brief: Pellacott's 2026 VA-220 valves are failing, and the leak-test certificates behind its score don't reflect real testing. The lab teardown found seat leakage with a deformed seal in 38 of 41 returned valves. Unused 2026 Pellacott valves leaked at the seat in 11% of a helium retest (44 of 400). Durrant-Hale valves showed none, and 2025 Pellacott valves almost none. When claims are matched to serial numbers, the failure rate is the same for new and legacy installers and for firmware 4.1 and 4.2, so installers and firmware are not the cause. The calibration contractor found Pellacott's only VA-220 leak rig out of service since 9 January 2026. Its last test was in December 2025. The 2026 certificates repeat four fixed sequences of values that also appear in November 2025 certificates. The score rose because complete-looking records earned credit, not because quality improved. Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates. Quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and release only after Brenmoor's own helium testing. Drop the installer remediation plan and chargebacks. Secure alternative supply, mainly Durrant-Hale, to avoid the line stoppage. The seal change and the line change cannot yet be separated, so reverting to Ferrand is premature. Whether other suppliers' records are also unreliable is unknown. Audit them promptly.

Pellacott's 2026-built VA-220 valves are failing, and the leak-test paperwork behind its better score does not reflect real testing. The installer and firmware explanations don't hold up.

The valve is the cause. Brenmoor's lab matched claims to valve source, installer and firmware. Pellacott valves fail at about 41–42 claims per 1,000 units whichever installer or firmware is involved. Durrant-Hale valves sit at 5–7 in every group. Never-installed Pellacott 2026 stock leaks at the seat in 11% of samples, against 0–1% for other stock.

The certificates are not real tests. The calibration contractor found the leak rig out of service since January, with no VA-220 test program on the other rigs. The per-piece tables repeat the same four sequences, some dating from before the rig failed. The score rose because the scorecard rewards complete-looking certificates.

What I don't know is whether the new seal supplier or the new assembly line is the root cause. The lab couldn't separate them. I also can't say whether other suppliers submitted similar records.

What to do now:
- Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates.
- Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock.
- Suspend Pellacott's dock-to-stock status.
- Release stock only after Brenmoor's own helium leak testing.
- Drop the installer remediation plan and chargebacks.
- Audit other suppliers' test records.

The fall in incidents is not real. Real confirmed incidents are running at about 36–37 a month, the same as before the migration. The audit trail shows that 47 of them (23 in September, 24 in October) were moved to "Suspicious Activity–Monitoring" after analysts had confirmed them. Each move came 3h31m–3h42m after the case opened, just after the 4-hour SLA warning flag. The change log shows a script on a Brackwater analyst jump host making these moves through the integration account. That account was given write access to every case field at Brackwater's request. The script polls for cases carrying the SLA-warning flag every five minutes. Moved cases drop out of the containment and SLA figures, which is why Brackwater reports 100% containment and why the monitoring queue has grown. None of the 47 has a containment timestamp. The cause is deliberate, not a platform fault, though I can't tell from this who ordered it. Do not sign off the retainer cut or the 60k bonus. Reinstate the 47 cases, have your team and Halvard verify containment on each, and remove the category-edit rights from the integration role. Then ask Brackwater for a written explanation. Hold off on claiming service credits until that is done. I haven't yet checked whether the 28 retired detection rules are missing attacks.

The rise in cancellations is mainly a Quillbook connector problem, not a price problem. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated invoices: 58,300 across 1,212 of the 1,900 Quillbook accounts. 34% of those accounts have cancelled, against 8% of Quillbook accounts with no failures. Churn among Quillbook-connected accounts went from about 2% to about 6%, and it is the same for repriced and price-locked Founders accounts. Accounts with no connector, about 7,200, barely moved (1.8% to 1.9%) whether repriced or not, and that holds in every seat band. The seat-band pattern in the finance analysis appears because larger accounts are more likely to use Quillbook. Price complaints in exit surveys are probably partly a stated reason for a deeper problem. Tallymarsh changes are small and within normal variation, though its log is unreviewed. Recommendation: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority (3–4 weeks), and contact all affected accounts, including those who have cancelled, to correct their invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold, since it has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books. Do not roll back the price now, and do not start the Tallymarsh rebuild; instead, review the Tallymarsh log first. Also consider support triage so that sync issues are not treated as Sev-3.

The whole rise sits in Quillbook-connected accounts, whose churn roughly tripled (about 2% to 6%) whether repriced or locked. The bigger-increase-leaves-more pattern appears because larger accounts are more likely to use Quillbook. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated invoices. 1,212 of 1,900 accounts were hit, and 34% of those have cancelled against 8% of unaffected accounts. These failures are logged as warnings, so the health panel never showed them. The 'price' answers in exit surveys are probably a stand-in for 'not worth it when invoices are wrong'. Tallymarsh numbers are tiny and within normal variation.

Next steps: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, 3–4 weeks. Contact all Quillbook accounts, including those that cancelled, to correct invoices. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold, because it protects customers' books. Don't roll back the price or start the Tallymarsh rebuild now. Review the Tallymarsh log cheaply first. Treat sync failures as high severity and fix the support response times. Confidence is fairly high.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a difference in time in level, not in work location. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so 215 of 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Only 32% of remote staff meet the 18-month eligibility rule, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, the nomination and approval rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote versus 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, and the observed rate is 7.6%. The dashboard's job-family split doesn't account for tenure, so it was misleading. Remote attrition is not higher (10.9% vs 11.6%).

Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It rests on a misread gap, and it would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts. Put it on hold, and report promotion rates for eligible staff only. Re-check at FY2027. The eligible remote group is small (110), so a gap of a few points can't be ruled out. Manager comments suggest remote staff may get fewer visible assignments, but nothing measured shows this. Check staffing records before acting on it. Briefings on promotion criteria are reasonable, since remote staff understand the criteria less well. Confidence is fairly high but not complete.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. The flag only works on build 7.4.0, so flagged users are all on 7.4.0 by design. Build 7.4.0 was already crashing at about 2% on 2–3 Sep, before the flag ramped, against about 0.7% on 7.3.2. Within 7.4.0, flagged users crash at 2.10% and the random flag-off holdout at 1.98%. That 0.12-point difference is within noise. Device memory mix and usage are similar across groups, so they don't explain it. The top 7.4.0 crash cluster is a native crash in the upgraded image library (Pixelda 3.1, HEIF decoding), which doesn't exist in 7.3.2. No top cluster contains canvas code. Both crash trackers show the same gap, so the new crash-reporting SDK isn't inventing it. The sync-service deploy doesn't fit either, because 7.3.2 stayed flat after 9 Sep. A small flag effect, a few tenths of a point at most, can't be ruled out yet. Don't turn the flag off and release 7.4.0 to everyone, because that would ship the real problem to 100% of users. Hold 7.4.0 at 25%, fix the Pixelda crash, and keep the flag holdout running (optionally widen it) to measure the small remaining flag effect.

Within 7.4.0, the flag-on group crashes 0.12 points more than the random flag-off holdout. That difference is within noise, so a small flag effect is not ruled out. Keep the flag holdout running, and widen it if you want an answer sooner. Don't roll back the SDK. I'm fairly sure of the main finding, less so on whether the flag has a small effect.

The evidence points mainly to Callerby's own decision, not Halden, as the cause of the slip. The tower crane and frame crew went to the Kestrel warehouse in October 2025, and the crane stayed away until April. The architect's register shows CO-09 was issued on 6 November, after the crane had already left. The other change orders were small interior layout changes. The platform's tamper-proof timestamps show the architect answered 62 of 64 information requests within the contract period. The 41 "late" requests in the draft claim were mostly sitting in Callerby's own draft status for 9–47 days before submission. The architect also answered the CO-09 structural query in four days. So do not submit the claim as drafted. It rests on a measure that overstates the architect's delay, and it would likely fail and damage credibility. The claim consultant's fee also depends on recovery, so their analysis should not be relied on. CO-09 may justify a small, properly evidenced extension, so have someone independent assess only that. Do not discipline the superintendent. He told the truth when asked, and a warning would discourage honesty. Do not suspend the incentive scheme yet. Nothing shows it drove the crane move. Still unknown: why the crane moved, and the steel delivery picture. I'm fairly sure about the claim's weakness, less sure about the full split of causes.

The jump in DC-stage write-offs is most likely caused by our own night receiving, not by Haverlow. The night team was cut from six to four on 27 July. Since then, median time from unloading to chamber has gone from 44 minutes to nearly 4 hours. Pallets sit on an unrefrigerated dock at 15–17°C. Night-shift write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% across all suppliers, while day shift stayed flat. Haverlow's trailer data shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when doors opened, with no alarms. The "warm" receipt probe readings are taken at confirmation, after the dock delay, so they measure our delay and not Haverlow's product. The chambers held temperature. Do not raise the chargeback or move volume: it would penalise the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Do not drop the night probe, which would hide the problem. Restore night staffing, or otherwise cut dock-to-chamber time, set a maximum time, and monitor it weekly from scan data. Separately, the Corriebank credit rise (from 3 August, self-certified claims) is unproven. Pull a sample of claims and match them to lots and receiving shift before changing terms. I am fairly confident in the main finding. I am less sure how much of the credit rise is over-claiming.

The rise in delayed alarm responses is most likely caused by the 12 August relay server move, not by agency nurses. The new server imported only 3 of the 14 forwarding rules. It lost the 15-second hold-off for brief SpO2 dips, the 60-second suppression of repeat alerts, and the routing of probe-off and leads-off alarms to the charge phone only. The import tool logged a warning but reported success. Pod D was still on the old server. Since 12 August, Pods A-C nurses get about 80 phone notifications per shift, up from about 38. Their acknowledgement time doubled. Pod D is unchanged. Delayed responses in Pods A-C rose about fourfold for core, agency and agency-equivalent staff alike. Pod D agency share is similar and Pod D incidents did not rise. The raw alarm rate from the monitors did not change, including after the 23-24 September software update. So acuity and the update are not the cause. Higher sick leave may be a consequence of the alarm load, but that link is not proven. Do not cap agency use or open performance reviews. Do not switch off phone alarms. Restore the 11 skipped rules with clinical validation, then track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Confidence is high. The Room 14 reports of phones not ringing should be checked separately.

The rise in delayed alarm responses is most likely caused by the 12 August move of the alert relay server, not by agency staff. The hardware move was meant to be like-for-like. But 11 of the 14 forwarding rules were silently skipped during import. Those rules included a 15-second hold-off on brief SpO2 alarms, suppression of repeat notifications, and routing of technical alarms to the charge phone only. Pods A–C then went from about 38 to about 82 phone notifications per nurse per shift, and acknowledgement time doubled from 34 s to 71 s. Pod D was still on the old server and shows no change. Incident rates rose equally for core, agency and new-graduate nurses, so this is not a staffing or individual-performance problem. Sick leave rising is probably linked to the virus season; a link to the alarm load is unproven. Recommendation: do not approve the agency cap or the performance reviews. Restore the 11 rules, with clinical validation, and track notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Wireless coverage was not directly checked, but Pod D's normal figures argue against a coverage problem. Confidence is high.

The rejections trace to a data error in our own systems, not to the fungicide, Lower Serra growers or Meridane. When Meridane bookings moved to the new Tallis system, the mandarin product record was copied from the avocado record on 1 Aug. It carried 7.0°C instead of our 4.0°C specification. All five Meridane containers were sent with a 7.0°C instruction, and the units held 7.0°C as told. All five were rejected. Every container at 4.0°C passed, including Coastway ones packed with the new fungicide. The one Meridane container at 4.0°C passed too, and the first rejection (K3) used the old fungicide. Lower Serra fruit looked worse within rejected containers, but it was 28–40% of every load and the temperature explains the pattern. Pallet-level data in accepted containers is missing, so I'm less sure about that. Do not suspend Lower Serra, switch fungicide back, or claim against Meridane, since its controller records support its reply. Next steps, urgently: correct the Tallis mandarin record to 4.0°C. Have Meridane reset the container at sea (sailed 3 Oct) and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a check comparing reefer settings with product specifications before submission. Review how the product master sign-off missed this. Tell Nordhafen about the cause and the fix.

Loggers are a reasonable extra. Any recovery from the contractor should wait for a proper review, because our own sign-off also missed the error. Confidence is high.

Other groups are at normal levels, and the firm-wide hours target applied to all of them, so neither a general market effect nor the target change explains this. Pay applies equally to Kestrel and non-Kestrel associates, yet almost only Kestrel people left, so pay looks unlikely to be the main driver. The survey comments point to heavy workload and to harsh feedback from supervisors.

What I can't tell you is whether the workload or Dorian Faulk's supervision is the cause. All 11 Kestrel associates report to him, and he supervises no one else, so the two can't be separated with the records I have. The farewell emails told me nothing. Confidence is moderate to high on "not pay, not the target, not ordinary market movement" and low on workload versus supervision.

Next steps: don't pay the £12k retention payment or close the review. Commission the roughly £9k confidential external interviews, designed to separate workload from supervision. Ask the interviewer to cover current Kestrel associates as well as leavers. Start tracking matter and supervising partner in attrition reporting. Hold off on moving supervision or hiring contract reviewers until the interviews report, because the document-review phase ends in December.

The rejects come from an interaction between two things. Arnholt resin arrives wetter than Quillan, and dryer D5 on Press 5 is degraded. Neither is a problem alone. Arnholt on Press 5 has about 10% rejects, in both shifts and for new and experienced operators alike. Arnholt on Press 7 (good dryer) is 0.8%. Quillan on Press 5 is 0.9%. Arnholt lot A-2291 dried in a good portable dryer and run on Press 5 gave 0.8% rejects. The same lot through D5 gave 10.4%. The second-shift gap exists because all second-shift VX runs on Press 5. The new operators are not the cause. Do not put them on improvement plans. The trial passed because it ran only on Press 7, and the certificates of analysis don't show the moisture actually measured. Do this week: repair D5 (heater and desiccant), restore the −40 alarm limit, and keep Arnholt off D5 until its dew point is verified. Add a feed-throat moisture check for every resin lot. Ask Arnholt about their moisture. Arnholt was only measured from the unconditioned north annex, so whether storage adds moisture is unproven. Don't pay for warehouse space until that is tested. I'm fairly confident in the main finding.

The rejects come from a combination: Arnholt resin dried in Press 5's dryer (D5), which is degraded. It is not the new operators and not Arnholt in general. On Press 5, Arnholt runs about 10% rejects against 0.9% for Quillan. On Press 7, Arnholt runs 0.8%. The six new hires reject at the same rate as experienced operators. Second shift looks worse only because all its VX runs on Press 5. D5's dew point is about −16 to −19 °C, and its alarm limit was loosened in week 31. Quillan resin starts drier, so it survived. Arnholt arrives wetter, at 0.27–0.33% at the dryer inlet, and D5 can't bring it under the 0.20% limit. The same Arnholt lot dried in a good portable dryer gave 0.8% rejects, against 10.4% through D5. So the cause is well established. What isn't known is why Arnholt arrives wetter. It may be north-annex storage or the supplier, and the samples can't separate the two. Do this week: repair D5 (heater and desiccant), restore the alarm limit, keep Arnholt off D5 until verified, and add a feed-throat moisture check for every lot. Don't discipline the operators or drop Arnholt. Hold off on renting space until a conditioned-storage test of the annex is done. Reply to the 8D with this finding.

Cancelling RotaWeave would not fix this, and neither would blaming the background checks. The drop is concentrated at Dock Street and Westgate, the two sites that have both the app and no coordinator. Millbrook has the app but kept its coordinator, and its numbers are steady. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but is not on the app yet, and it is also steady. The basic app tier releases shifts to everyone each Thursday, and it has no recurring bookings. Coordinators used to hold regulars' usual slots. Since 1 May, bookings made on regulars' behalf have fallen from 74 a week to 3. Of 213 April regulars at those two sites, 129 lost their usual slot at least twice, mostly to new or corporate sign-ups. 88% of them are now inactive, against 11% of those who kept their slot. The background-check deadline hit all sites equally. 121 of the 123 who lapsed held a current check. Commonplate was barely involved, since only 2 callbacks mention another group. Next steps: assign someone to book regulars into their usual slots before each Thursday release, using the unused admin seat. Phone lapsed regulars and offer their slots back, and review after 60 days. Hold off on cancelling the contract, suspending checks or removing inactive names from the roster. Confidence is fairly high but rests on observational data.

The Android login drop is not caused by app release 6.14, the phone security patch, or bots. It comes from a new Corvane edge rule, AUTO-LIB-17, which went live on 3 March at 10:38 UTC. The rule blocks password logins from the app's networking library. Blocks began at 10:41 on every app version, and the bank's telemetry shows the added failures as HTTP 403 on password submissions only. Quick-unlock is unaffected, and iOS and web don't match the rule. About 41,300 installs were blocked, and 92% of them had logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, so these are real customers. I'm confident in this diagnosis: the timing, the 403 errors and the blocked-request log all agree.

Next steps:
1. Ask Corvane today to set AUTO-LIB-17 to log-only, or exempt requests with the Android client header, on the password path. Keep rate limits, lockout and other rules active.
2. Confirm in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%.
3. Don't roll back 6.14, and don't raise bot sensitivity. Don't remove blocked attempts from the KPI, because that would hide a real customer outage.
4. Ask Corvane to give notice and let the bank test vendor rule changes before they go live.
5. Revisit the call-volume link separately. Fee notices also drove calls that week.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by the vendor's 3 March edge rule-pack update, not by release 6.14. A new rule (AUTO-LIB-17) blocks password-login requests that carry the nettle-http user-agent and have no edge session cookie. The Android app uses that library for all its API calls, so the rule blocks the app's own password logins with HTTP 403. Evidence: the extra failures began at 10:41 UTC on 3 March, one minute after the rule activated. They appear on every app version, including the 95% of users still on older versions, and on every Android OS version, whether or not the March patch is installed. Quick-unlock is unaffected, and iOS and web are unaffected. About 41,300 blocked installs had mostly logged in successfully before, so these are real customers, not bots. Only 5% of attempts were on 6.14 at first. Rolling back 6.14 would not help.
Next steps: ask Corvane to switch that rule to log-only on the password path, keeping rate limits, lockout and other rules on, then check that password success returns to about 96%. Don't raise bot sensitivity or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI. Tell the Head of Digital Channels that no rollback is needed. Contact-centre call volume is only loosely tied to this, since fee notices were also mailed that week.

The fall in first-contact resolution is almost certainly due to the 14 April Finance change, not the new starters. It cut the credit an agent can apply on a call from £100 to £25. Larger adjustments now go automatically to the Billing Resolution team. The share of billing calls referred rose from 7% to 54% in the week of 14 April. Referred calls resolve at about 33%, against 82% for the rest. This closely matches the timing and size of the drop. New starters refer at the same rate as tenured agents (56% vs 53–54%). Tenured agents' FCR fell from about 75% to 67%, the same as the site, so the intake is not the cause. Tariff-enquiry call mix barely changed. Performance plans for the April intake would punish the wrong group, so don't do them. I'm less sure about the IVR and workload effects, because I did not examine them directly. Next step: agree a revised in-call credit limit with Finance, with post-call sampling of credits. Trial it on two teams for six weeks. Track FCR and the unsupported-credit rate. Finance has said it would accept this kind of trial. A rollout to everyone at once is premature. Rebuilding the dashboard is useful but not urgent.

The evidence doesn't support blaming the Admissions Office for the enrolment drop. Applications and admits rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield (admits who enrolled) fell about 7 points in both rounds. That includes early action, which was handled on the old system and on the usual schedule, so the late regular-decision answers can't explain most of the fall. The clearest pattern is by scholarship tier. Yield collapsed only in the Dean's tier (award cut from $14,000 to $9,000) and the Merit tier ($9,000 to $5,000). It held steady in the Presidential tier, where awards were unchanged, and among students with no merit award. The October 2025 award cut is the most likely cause, and the finance committee judged its yield effect on an outdated 2021 estimate. The slow regular-decision turnaround and the portal problems were real service failures, and they may have cost individual students, but they don't explain the overall drop. Replacing the director on this basis would punish the wrong party. Next steps: take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal for the affected tiers, and set a turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until missing documents are verified. I'm fairly confident in the main conclusion. The size of the delay effect is uncertain.

Don't roll back the gateway. The latency jump comes from the 2 Nov storage compaction tuning change, not release 5.8. Eleven cells got the config push at about 23:38–23:52 and each jumped to ~300 ms p99 within minutes, regardless of when 5.8 reached it. aps-3 got 5.8 but skipped the push and stayed at ~94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing (291 → 297 → 293 ms). On the storage nodes, compaction threads went from 2 to 6, disks went from 41% to 97% busy, and node-side read time rose from 61 to 262 ms. Network and traffic growth don't explain it: GET traffic rose only 6%, and aps-3 saw similar growth without a regression. A rollback would also reopen the security hole and hit the 30 Nov audit deadline for nothing. Next: revert the compaction tuning in one cell, watch GET p99 and backlog, then extend to the rest. Backlog is 11% against a ~15% danger line, so watch it, and don't pause compaction. Hold off on throttling Orrin until the 10 Nov attribution report shows what is driving backlog growth. Confidence is high on cause, moderate on what is driving the backlog.

Store 14's rise is not yet shown to be a real change in losses. The Q1–Q3 figures are estimates from partial cycle counts, with a margin of about ±0.6 points per quarter. In past years, about half of stores with two straight rises were not confirmed by the full count. Store 14's full-count shrink has stayed at 1.5–1.8% for three years. The shoplifting log counts are weak evidence: the incident app launched chain-wide on 1 April, and recorded incidents rose across the chain while chain shrink stayed flat. The ethics-line tip was checked against CCTV and the stocker was carrying cardboard bales, so suspending him would be unjustified. The sales mix did not change, so that explanation is out. The self-checkout lanes and the bus interchange both coincide with the rise, but neither is shown to cause it. Neighbouring stores show no matching trend, though that comparison is weak. Recommendation: keep store 14 in the 7 December full count and decline Regional Operations' request to drop it. Hold off on a guard, on pulling or staffing the lanes, and on any action against the stocker until the count result is compared with the interim figures. Then act on what it shows. I'm fairly confident in this, but I haven't ruled out a real loss problem.

The rise from 0.31% to 0.41% looks like ordinary week-to-week variation. Over the previous 26 weeks the rate averaged 0.354% and the policy's upper limit is 0.482%. Several earlier weeks were higher (0.51%, 0.47%, 0.45%), and investigating them found nothing. The dashboard count matches raw logs, so it is not a counting artefact. The burn rate is 0.82x against a 2x page threshold. Bookings and support complaints did not change.

The "new pods error twice as often" finding is a warm-up effect. Any new pod starts with an empty cache, so its first minutes produce timeouts. Every recent rollout shows the same gap, including a config-only redeploy with no code change. That adds only about 10–20 errors, so it says nothing about v4.18 being faulty.

What I could not settle is whether the replica move or partner-sync month-end traffic added a little. Neither looks needed to explain the week.

Next steps: don't roll back and don't mute alerts. Note the week at ops review and apply the normal check to the following week. If that week is above 0.48%, open an incident then. Confidence is fairly high, about 80%.

Next: revert the 5.2 adaptive-streaming settings in Kestria, hold the wider rollout, and have the app team find the fault. The rise is very likely not a handling problem. Since 1 September, tags printed on the new Fennick stock fail automatic reading about 12% of the time, against about 1.5% before. Those bags go to the manual encode desk, where waits rose from 7 to about 30 minutes in the evening bank. They reach the lateral after the cart has closed and miss the flight. Bags that read automatically are as reliable as before (about 3.8 per 1,000). Pelion, handled by the same Tessaly crew pool, did not worsen. On 14–16 Oct, counters briefly using old Brackwater stock failed at 1.6% while kiosks on Fennick failed at 12.1%. Transfer tags and Pelion tags read normally, so the airport's readers are not at fault.

What is unclear is whether the stock itself is faulty or whether the printers need different heat settings for it. Kiosk cleaning also became less frequent.

Next steps: do not send the breach notice or withhold the fee. Switch back to Brackwater stock now (about five weeks are in stores and the contract is valid to 31 Dec). Then test Fennick stock with the printer maker's settings before making any claim against Fennick. Asking HBAA for an extra encode workstation in the evening is a reasonable stopgap. I'm fairly confident in this.

Don't discipline anyone or retrain on braking. The evidence points to contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique, the hills, or the pads. Northfield Motor Services serviced 13 Eastgate vans while our own brake bay was closed. Eleven of them drew all 27 soft-pedal complaints. Northfield used a bulk fluid drum opened in March whose cap had gone missing. Their own tests on two returned vans showed fluid boiling at about 150°C, against 255°C for sealed stock. The two Northfield vans serviced from a new drum had no complaints. The same drivers ran 604 days in other vans, 141 of them on Upper Wend, with no brake reports. Calder Road vans, with the same pads and the same hills, had none either. The Northfield email recommending rechecks on 25 Sep went unanswered, and the coordinator is on leave.

What to do this week: take all 13 Northfield-serviced vans off the road, test the fluid and renew it from sealed stock, then return them to service. Ask Northfield to confirm which other Larkspur vans used that drum. Withdraw the proposed warnings, because drivers were reporting a real fault. Hold off on changing pad supplier; the squeal data is confounded by fresh pads. I am fairly confident (about 85–90%). Testing the Calder-serviced vans at their next service is a reasonable low-priority extra.

The most likely cause is contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique or the new pads. Northfield Motor Services serviced 13 Eastgate vans while the in-house bay was closed. Eleven of them were filled from an old bulk drum that had lost its cap and had stood open since March. Two vans from that garage were later tested: the fluid boiled at about 150°C, against 255°C for sealed stock. That fits a pedal that goes soft on long descents. Upper Wend is the trigger that exposes the weak fluid, not the root cause. Calder Road Garage fitted the same Tessaro pads and used sealed fluid. None of its 12 vans has a soft-pedal complaint, and the Calder job cards show no returns. That counts against the pads. Confidence is fairly high but not complete, because I have not matched each complaint van to its garage. Northfield flagged the risk on 25 Sep and got no reply.

This week:
1. Take every Northfield-serviced van out of service.
2. Test its fluid and renew it from sealed stock.
3. Do not issue warnings or run blanket retraining. Drivers reported a real fault, and discipline would suppress reports.
4. Hold off on changing pad supplier.
5. Confirm which vans went to which garage.

The wrong dates were not caused by operators or by the printer firmware. The Veltranol shelf-life record in the ERP got a new 36-month value on 3 Oct. It was entered under CC-309 and was meant to apply only from 1 Mar 2027. From 4 Oct, the data sent to the printers carried 36 months, so the printed expiry came out 12 months late. The printer records show this. Before 4 Oct every job used 24 months and was correct, including jobs run by the new agency operators after the firmware change. After 4 Oct no operator overrode anything, and the camera passed every carton because it only checks print against the job. Two lots on Line 1 day shift were also affected, so this is not just Line 3 nights or agency staff.

I'm fairly sure of the cause. I'm not sure why the integration service used a value it should have ignored. The vendor says it can't, so ask them to explain.

Next steps:
- Don't discipline or remove the agency operators.
- Reset the Veltranol shelf-life records.
- Hold every Veltranol lot packed since 4 Oct, including the two in the warehouse.
- Add a second-person check of printed expiry against the batch record at each setup.
- Check retained cartons for HX-15-30 and MR-05-14, whose changes also have future start dates.
- Hold off on a 12-month site-wide review and on over-labelling other products until those checks show a wider problem.

Floors 1-5 were flat overall. Of the 74 negative comments, 56 were about heat, all from floors 6-8. Don't serve notice on Orrin and don't pull the kiosks. Don't exclude the floor 6-8 responses from the reported score either; that would hide a real failure. Guests on floors 6-8 already got apologies and credits, so any further return-stay offer is optional. I'm fairly confident in this, though the rate-rise effect is unresolved.

Pellacott's 2026-built VA-220 valves are failing, and the cause is not the new installers or firmware 4.2. The Quality Lab matched claims by serial number. Pellacott valves fail at the same rate (about 40 per 1,000) regardless of installer or firmware. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. A helium retest of unused warehouse stock found 11% of Pellacott's 2026 valves leaking at the seat. The independent calibration visit found Pellacott's only VA-220 leak rig out of service since 9 Jan 2026, with no VA-220 test program on any other rig. Certificate tables repeat four sequences that also appear in 2025 certificates, so the certificates do not reflect tests that were done. The score rose because complete-looking certificates earn credit, which is how the score and the failures moved in opposite directions. Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates. Quarantine 2026 Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and release stock only after Brenmoor's own helium testing. Hold the installer remediation plan and the chargebacks. Then audit other suppliers' test records, and make scoring credit test records only when rig logs or witnessed tests back them. The seal supplier and Line 3 effects can't be separated yet, so treat them as open and have Pellacott's change reviewed.

The rise in cancellations is mostly not a pricing problem. It comes from Quillbook invoice-sync failures that began when Quillbook retired its old interface on 30 March. Accounts with no connector, repriced or not, barely moved (1.8% to 1.9%). Quillbook accounts rose from about 2% to about 6%, whether or not they had the price lock. Of the 1,212 Quillbook accounts that had sync failures, 34% cancelled, against 8% of those with none. The failures are logged as warnings, so the health panel misses them. The price-size pattern in the finance analysis is explained by larger accounts being more likely to use Quillbook. Tallymarsh changes are too small to tell apart from normal variation. I'm fairly confident, around 85–90%.

Recommendation:

The price rise is probably not the main cause of the extra cancellations. The cancellations are concentrated in accounts connected to Quillbook. Their monthly churn went from about 2% to about 6%, and this was the same whether the account paid the new price or kept the old locked price. Accounts with no connector barely changed (1.8% to 1.9%), even the big-seat ones. The larger-account pattern the finance team saw mostly reflects Quillbook accounts having more seats. Quillbook retired an old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then, invoices have gone missing or been duplicated for 1,212 accounts, and 34% of those have cancelled, against 8% of accounts with no recorded failure. The fault is logged as a warning, so the health panel doesn't show it, and the fix is unscheduled and rated low severity.

Next steps:

The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not a location effect. Remote hiring only opened to all roles in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: 230 of 340 haven't reached the 18 months in level that the policy requires to be nominated, against 200 of 760 office staff. Among eligible staff, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%) and approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) are almost the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, close to the observed 7.6%. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job mix isn't the cause. I'm fairly confident, though the eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a modest real bias can't be ruled out. Stretch-assignment access is unmeasured; the manager comments hint at it but don't establish it. Don't adopt the three-day office rule: it would penalise about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Instead, put it on hold, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Consider pulling staffing records to test the stretch-work question.

The evidence doesn't support the claim that proximity bias explains the gap. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level that the promotion policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote vs 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote group's eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, and the observed rate is 7.6%. The remote group is mostly newer hires, which is consistent with the manager's comment that his remote staff haven't been with the company long. The remaining 1.1-point difference rests on 110 people and could be chance. Don't confirm proximity bias, and don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts for a gap that is mostly about tenure. I could not test whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments, because the staffing system doesn't record it. I also didn't check whether remote staff leave at higher rates or why more remote staff are recent hires. Next steps: put the rule on hold, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Meanwhile, start collecting data on who gets stretch work. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding and low on the secondary questions.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Everyone on build 7.4.0 crashes about 2% of sessions, versus about 0.7% on 7.3.2. That was already true on 2–3 Sep, before the flag ramped. Only 7.4.0 users can get the flag, so the flag group is simply the 7.4.0 group. Among 7.4.0 users, flag-on is 2.10% and a random flag-off holdout is 1.98%. That difference is small and within noise. The leading crash cluster (41%) is a native crash in the upgraded image library (Pixelda 3.1) HEIF decoding. It first appeared on 2 Sep and is absent from 7.3.2. The app-store console's own crash counts show the same gap, so the crash-reporting SDK change isn't a counting artifact. Device mix, usage and the 9 Sep backend deployment don't explain it. A small flag effect, a few tenths of a point, can't be ruled out. Turning the flag off and releasing 7.4.0 to 100% would ship the real problem. Recommendation: hold 7.4.0 at 25%, fix the image-library crash, and keep the existing holdout running (widening it would speed up the measurement). Don't rework the canvas yet. I'm fairly confident in this, though less so on whether the flag has any effect.

The rise in write-offs is not a Haverlow problem. It comes from the night receiving cut. Haverlow's trailer data shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened, and the trailers were empty by about 23:00–23:40. The warm readings (6.6–7.9°C) were keyed at 02:31–03:18, hours after unloading. Since the night team went from six to four people, median time from dock to chamber has gone from 44 minutes to about 3h50. Product sits in unrefrigerated staging at roughly 15–17°C. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, while day shift stayed flat. The chambers are holding temperature. Don't raise the chargeback or move volume. It would penalise a supplier whose product arrived cold, and it would leave the cause in place. Don't drop the night probe either, since it is the check that shows the problem. Restore the night team to six, set a maximum dock-to-chamber time, and track it weekly from scan data. Separately, request Corriebank's claim-level extract and check a sample of claims before changing their credit terms. Their credits rose after self-certification began, but part of that rise may be real spoilage from the warm dock. I'm fairly confident in the main diagnosis. The share of credits that are over-claims remains unknown.

Regular volunteers are leaving because of the two changes together, not the app alone. The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a new vendor edge rule, not by release 6.14. A Corvane rule pack went live on 3 March at 10:38 UTC. It added rule AUTO-LIB-17, which blocks (HTTP 403) password requests whose user-agent is the networking library nettle-http and that carry no edge session cookie. Our Android app uses that library for every call. The failures began at 10:41 on every app version within a minute, which shows the 6.14 rollout is not the cause. That rollout was only 5% of attempts, and the older versions fail at the same rate. Quick-unlock and iOS are unaffected. The blocked traffic comes from about 41,300 installs, and 92% of them had a successful login in the previous 90 days, so these are real customers, not bots. OS patch level makes no difference. Do not roll back 6.14. Do not raise bot sensitivity. Do not exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, because that would hide the problem. Next, ask Corvane to set the AUTO-LIB-17 rule to log-only on the mobile password path. Keep rate limits, lockout and the other rules active. Then confirm in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Let the 6.14 rollout continue while you track outcomes by app version. I'm quite confident. The link to the extra call volume is unproven, because the fee mailing is a competing explanation.

The latency regression is not caused by gateway 5.8. It comes from the compaction tuning change pushed to storage nodes on the evening of 2 Nov. After that push, each cell's disk utilisation went from about 41% to 97% within minutes. Disk read wait rose from 9 to 205 ms, and node-side GET time rose from 61 to 262 ms. Every cell that got the push degraded within minutes, whatever its gateway version. One cell, aps-3, skipped the push, even though it had 5.8, and stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. Network and traffic growth don't explain it. I'm fairly sure of this, about 90%.

Don't roll back the gateway. That would reopen the signature security flaw and wouldn't fix latency. Don't pause compaction, because the backlog would grow toward disk-full. Instead, revert the tuning change in one cell, watch p99 and backlog, then extend it to the other cells. Consider pacing Orrin's migration later, once the 10 Nov backlog attribution report is in. Look for a middle setting that keeps backlog under 15% without saturating disks. Fleet config pushes should also go on the shared change calendar.

The "new pods error twice as often" finding is a normal warm-up effect. Every recent rollout, including a config-only redeploy, shows the same gap, caused by empty caches on new pods. I'm fairly confident in this, though I did not test the replica move or partner-sync traffic directly. Neither is needed for the decision.

Next steps: don't roll back, and don't mute alerting. That would remove the protection for no benefit. Note the week at ops review, apply the standard check to the following week, and escalate only if that week exceeds the band or the burn-rate page fires.

The brake complaints are very likely caused by contaminated brake fluid, not by drivers, the hills or the new pads. During the workshop closure, Northfield Motor Services changed the fluid in 13 of your vans. Eleven of them got fluid from an old bulk drum with a missing cap that had taken on water. Those 11 vans are exactly the 11 vans with soft-pedal complaints. The two vans that got fluid from a new drum have no complaints. Two vans retested on 24 September had fluid boiling at about 150°C, against 255°C for fresh fluid. Fluid that takes on water can vaporise on long descents, which makes the pedal go soft. The same drivers ran Upper Wend in other vans, 141 days in all, with no brake reports. Tessaro pads were fitted at both garages and in-house, so they don't explain it.

What to do this week: pull the 11 vans from Northfield's bulk drum (and, to be safe, all 13 Northfield-serviced vans) off the road. Test and renew their fluid from sealed stock, then return them. Do not discipline drivers or start retraining. Also check what the other garage, Calder Road, used. I'm fairly confident, about 85–90%. The squeal link to the Tessaro pads is still unresolved, so hold off on changing pad supplier.

The rise in cancellations is mostly a Quillbook connector problem, not a pricing problem. Quillbook retired its old invoice interface on 30 March. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated 58,300 invoices across 1,212 accounts. 34% of those accounts have cancelled, against 8% of Quillbook accounts with no failures. Recommendation: make the Quillbook v3 fix the top engineering priority, and contact all Quillbook accounts, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices. Don't roll back the price: it would cost about $220k a month and wouldn't address the cause. Keep the duplicate-invoice hold on. Hold off on the Tallymarsh rebuild until someone reviews its log. The gap looks mostly like a difference in time in level, not a proximity effect. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination and approval rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote versus 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. The gap also appears in every job family, so job mix isn't the cause. The remaining 1.1-point difference rests on only 110 remote staff, so a small real bias can't be ruled out. Stretch-work access is unmeasured: the staffing system can't show it. Attrition wasn't examined, so I can't say whether remote staff leave more often. I'm fairly confident about the main finding, less so about the smaller points. Don't confirm proximity bias or announce the three-day office rule. It targets the wrong cause, and about 180 remote staff on home-based contracts live too far away to comply. Instead, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Meanwhile, start tracking stretch assignments, and check why remote staff are newer. Briefings on the criteria are a reasonable low-cost addition.

Next steps: put the rule on hold, change the dashboard to compare eligible employees only, and track stretch-work allocation so you can re-check at FY2027. Prioritise a fix for the Pixelda crash. Keep the existing holdout running (or widen it) to settle the flag question. Don't roll back the SDK.

The dock averages 15–17°C overnight. Night-shift write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label alike, while day-shift rates stayed flat. Haverlow's trailer data shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors open. The warm receiving readings are taken after the long dock wait, so they don't show what arrived. The chambers are holding temperature. The chargeback and volume move would punish the wrong party, so don't do them. Instead, restore night receiving staffing, or otherwise fix dock-to-chamber time, and set a maximum time monitored weekly. Probe pallets at unload, not at confirmation. Dropping the night probe would hide the problem. Separately, Corriebank's rise in credits started when self-certification began, but that rise may also be partly real spoilage from the warm dock. Pull a sample of claims and reconcile them before changing credit terms. I'm fairly confident in the main cause. The Corriebank share is unresolved.

Every Meridane container booked through Tallis (K3, K4, K6, K8, K9) was sent at 7.0°C and ran at 7.0°C, and every one was rejected. Next steps, in order: (1) Correct the mandarin record in Tallis today. (2) Have Meridane reset the container at sea and the one queued for 10 Oct to 4.0°C. Independent loggers are a reasonable extra safeguard. Review the sign-off process, not individual blame.

The rejects come from the combination of Arnholt resin and Press 5's degraded dryer (D5). Neither alone causes them. On Press 5, Arnholt lots reject at about 10%, against 0.9% for Quillan. Arnholt on Press 7, which has a healthy dryer, rejects at 0.8%. The new operators are not the cause: second shift runs only on Press 5, and every operator group rejects about 10% on Arnholt and 0.9% on Quillan. Arnholt arrives wetter, at 0.27–0.33% moisture against 0.11–0.14% for Quillan. D5 can't dry it below the 0.20% limit. In a week-42 test, the same Arnholt lot dried in a good dryer gave 0.8% rejects, against 10.4% through D5. The Arnholt trial ran only on Press 7, so it could never have exposed this. Quillan alone was tolerable on D5. I'm quite confident in this. One caveat: all Arnholt resin was stored in the north annex, so I can't separate Arnholt's own wetness from the storage effect. Do not discipline the operators and do not drop Arnholt. This week, repair D5 (heater and desiccant), restore the original alarm limit, and keep Arnholt off D5 until its dew point is verified at −40 °C. Add a moisture check at the press feed throat for every resin lot. Test conditioned storage for Arnholt separately before spending on warehouse space.

Through D5 it reaches the press at about 0.25–0.31%, above the 0.20% limit. That causes splay and latch cracks. Press 5 on Arnholt rejects about 9.9%. Press 5 on Quillan rejects 0.9%. Press 7 on Arnholt rejects 0.8%. The same Arnholt lot dried in a good portable dryer gave 0.8%, against 10.4% through D5. The Android drop is almost certainly caused by a new Corvane edge rule, not by release 6.14. The 3 March rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17) that blocks password requests carrying the nettle-http user-agent. That is the library every Android version uses. Blocking began at 10:41 UTC on 3 March, about three minutes after the rule pack activated. The same drop appears on every app version, including 6.11 and older, and on every OS version, whether or not the March security patch is installed. Quick-unlock, iOS and web are unaffected. Password success fell from 96% to 8%. About 41,300 install IDs were blocked, and 92% of them had logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, so these are real customers and not bots. So a rollback of 6.14 would not help. Raising bot sensitivity would block more customers. Dropping blocked attempts from the KPI would hide the problem. Next step: ask Corvane today to set the rules added in 2026.03.1 to log-only on the mobile password-login path. Keep rate limits, lockout and all other rules active. Then confirm in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Continue the 6.14 rollout while you do. I'm fairly confident, around 90%.

The latency jump is not caused by gateway 5.8. It was caused by the storage compaction tuning change pushed on the evening of 2 Nov. Evidence: in 11 cells the push raised compaction threads from 2 to 6. Disk use went from 41% to 97% within minutes, and node-side GET time went from 61 ms to 262 ms. Each cell's latency jumped within about 5–10 minutes of its own push, regardless of when 5.8 arrived. Cell aps-3 received 5.8 but skipped the push, and its latency stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. The network is clean. A fleet-wide rollback would not fix latency and would reopen the security flaw, which has a 30 Nov audit deadline. Do not pause compaction. Instead, revert the tuning in one cell first and watch GET p99 and backlog, then extend to the other cells. Compaction is still needed, since backlog is 4.0% now and the 15% danger point is not expected before 13 Nov. Hold off on limiting Orrin until the 10 Nov attribution report. Confidence is high, and the one-cell revert is the cheap confirming test.

The evidence points to contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique. Northfield Motor Services serviced 13 Eastgate vans between 4 Aug and 12 Sep. Eleven of them used fluid from an old bulk drum that had lost its cap and was left open. It was later tested at about 150°C boiling point, against 255°C for fresh fluid. That drum is the likely source of water in the fluid, which can make the pedal go soft on long descents. Those 11 vans are exactly the 11 vans in the complaints. The two Northfield vans that got fluid from a new drum had no complaints. The same drivers drove other vans on the same hilly routes with no brake reports. Tessaro pads were fitted to the problem vans and the clean vans alike, so pads don't explain the pattern. Northfield recommended rechecking the other vans on 25 Sep and got no reply.
Next steps:
1. Pull the 11 vans from service. Test their fluid and renew it from sealed stock.
2. Check the vans Calder Road Garage serviced, and the other Northfield vans, as a precaution.
3. Drop the warnings and retraining. They would punish drivers who reported a real fault and would discourage reporting.
4. Leave the supplier decision until there is evidence on pads.
I'm fairly confident (about 85–90%). Testing the fluid in the vans would confirm it.

The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote hiring only opened in July 2024, so 215 of 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Only 32% of remote staff meet the policy's 18-month eligibility rule, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly identical: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job-family mix doesn't explain it. I'm fairly confident, though the eligible remote group is small (110), so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Some visibility effects are plausible: managers hand urgent work to people sitting nearby, and remote staff are less likely to feel leaders know their work. We have no assignment data to test that. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Put it on hold. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Also collect stretch-assignment data, and explain the promotion criteria to remote staff.

The crash gap is mostly not caused by the Tiled Canvas flag. Only 7.4.0 can receive the flag, and 7.4.0 crashes at about 2% versus about 0.7% on 7.3.2. Within 7.4.0, flag-on users (2.10%) and the random flag-off holdout (1.98%) are close, and the difference is within noise. Device mix and usage are about the same across groups. Turning the flag off and releasing 7.4.0 to 100% would spread the real crash problem to everyone while closing the incident. Hold 7.4.0 at 25%, and fix the Pixelda crash first (check the library upgrade and HEIF decoding). Keep the existing holdout running, and consider widening it to settle the flag question sooner. Don't roll back the crash-reporting SDK. I'm fairly confident, though the Pixelda cause is not directly proven.

Every Meridane container booked through Tallis (K3, K4, K6, K8, K9) was sent at 7.0°C, ran at that temperature, and was rejected with 9–14% decay. Every container booked at 4.0°C passed, including K5 and K7 on the new fungicide, and K1 on Meridane's route. It may be a secondary effect, and it doesn't explain the rejections. I'm quite confident. Next steps: correct PRD-MAND-01 to 4.0°C today. Have Meridane reset the container at sea (sailed 3 Oct) and the one queued for 10 Oct. Add a check of reefer settings against the product spec before submission. Review the product-master sign-off. Hold the cargo claim, the Lower Serra suspension and the fungicide reversal. Loggers in containers are reasonable as a short-term safeguard.

The rejects come from an interaction between two things. Arnholt resin arrives wetter than Quillan (0.27–0.33% against 0.11–0.14%). Dryer D5 has degraded, with a dew point of about −16 °C instead of −40 °C. D5 can't dry Arnholt below the 0.20% limit, so Press 5 makes cracked and splayed parts. Rates by press and resin:
- Press 5 on Arnholt: 9.9% rejects.
- Press 5 on Quillan: 0.9%.
- Press 7 on Arnholt: 0.8%.
- Press 7 on Quillan: 0.7%.
The same Arnholt lot gave 10.4% rejects through D5 and 0.8% through a good dryer.

Second shift only looks worse because all its VX work runs on Press 5. Within that shift, new and experienced operators have the same rates. Don't discipline the new operators, and don't drop Arnholt.

Do this week:
1. Repair D5, meaning the heater and desiccant.
2. Restore the alarm limit that was loosened to −15.
3. Keep Arnholt off D5 until D5 is verified.
4. Check moisture at the press feed throat for every resin lot.

Answer the 8D with this cause. I'm quite confident in this cause. One thing is unresolved: whether the north annex storage is why Arnholt arrives wetter. Every Arnholt sample came from the annex, so supplier and storage can't be separated. Moving the octabins is premature. Check Arnholt moisture in sealed packaging first.

The evidence points away from blaming RotaWeave alone, the background checks, or Commonplate. The basic app tier has no recurring bookings. Coordinators used to book regulars into their usual slots (about 74 a week before May, 3 a week since). Regulars then lost their slots to new sign-ups: 88% of those who lost a slot twice or more are now inactive, against 11% of those who kept theirs. Almost all of those who lapsed had current background checks, and only 2 of 61 callbacks mentioned another group. I'm fairly confident, with the caveat that the booking data comes from a single manager. Next steps: have staff or a trained lead volunteer book regulars into their usual slots before each Thursday release at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed regulars to offer their slots back. Don't cancel RotaWeave, suspend the checks, or purge the roster. Quarry Lane's October go-live needs the same protection.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by the vendor's edge rule update on 3 March, not by release 6.14. A new rule (AUTO-LIB-17) blocks requests from the app's networking library on the password-login path. It started at 10:41 UTC, about three minutes after the rule pack went live. It returns 403 to roughly 9,600 requests a day, and 92% of the blocked installs are existing, legitimate customers. The drop is identical on every app version, including old ones that were not updated. It is identical on every OS version, patched or not. Quick-unlock, iOS and web are unaffected, and the failures started at the rule time rather than at the 3 March 09:00 rollout start. Credential stuffing, the OS patch and the token-lifetime change don't fit the pattern. Rolling back 6.14 or reverting the password screen would not help. Raising bot sensitivity would block more customers. Excluding blocked attempts from the KPI would hide the real problem. Next step: ask Corvane to put the rules added on 3 March into log-only mode on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockout and other rules on. Then confirm in telemetry that password success recovers to about 96%. Ask Corvane for a proper fix, and make vendor rule updates subject to testing. The call-volume link is plausible but not proven, since fee notices went out the same week.

The latency regression comes from the storage compaction tuning change (FC-7710), not from gateway 5.8. The change raised compaction threads from 2 to 6. Compaction's share of disk bytes rose from 38% to 71%. Disk use went from 41% to 97% within 5 minutes of the push, and node-side GET time rose from 61 ms to 262 ms. In every cell that received the change, p99 jumped within minutes, whatever gateway version it ran. The cell that skipped the change, aps-3, got gateway 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. A test rollback of euw-1 to 5.7 changed nothing. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing. I'm fairly confident, around 90%. Don't roll back the gateway. Doing so would reopen the security hole and wouldn't fix latency. Don't pause compaction either, because backlog would grow toward disk-full. Instead, revert the tuning in one cell first and watch p99 and backlog, then extend to the other cells if it works. Consider a more moderate compaction setting afterwards. Hold off on limiting Orrin's ingest. The 10 Nov attribution job will show what drove the backlog, and the projection says backlog won't reach 15% before 13 Nov. Gateway CPU profiling is low priority.

The remote promotion gap is mostly a difference in who was eligible, not evidence of bias against remote staff. Under the policy, people need 18 months in their level to be nominated. Only 32% of remote staff meet that, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates are almost the same (28.2% remote, 28.6% office). Approval rates are also close (71% remote, 74% office). Eligible promotion rates are 20.0% remote and 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. The remaining gap of about one point rests on only 110 remote people, so it could be chance, and I can't rule out a small real effect. The dashboard's "every job family" pattern is likely the same tenure effect repeated in each family. I did not test the stretch-assignment concern or whether remote staff leave more often. Both are still open. Do not adopt the three-day office rule. It rests on a misread comparison and would hit about 180 remote hires on home-based contracts. Put it on hold. Change reporting to compare eligible people only, and re-check at FY2027. Meanwhile, look at stretch-work allocation and attrition. Confidence is moderate to high.

Cancelling RotaWeave is not supported by the evidence. The drop comes from two changes acting together. On the basic tier, a regular keeps a weekly slot only if staff book it before the Thursday release. Until 30 April, staff booked about 74 slots a week at Dock Street and Westgate. After the coordinator posts ended on 1 May, that fell to 3 a week, and one admin seat has sat unused. Regulars lost their usual slots to new sign-ups. Of 213 April regulars there, 129 lost a slot at least twice, and 88% of those are now inactive. Only 11% of those who kept their slot are inactive. Millbrook has the app and a coordinator, and it is stable. Quarry Lane lost its coordinator but has no app and a paper roster kept by the lead volunteer, and it is also stable. The background check does not explain the drop: 121 of the 123 who lapsed had a current check, and 21 of the 23 deactivated were reactivated. Commonplate is a minor factor: 2 of the 61 people reached by callback joined another group. What to do: have a staff member or trained lead volunteer book regulars into their usual slots at Dock Street and Westgate, and phone lapsed regulars to offer their slot back. Do not cancel the contract, suspend the checks, or purge the roster. My confidence is fairly high. The data is observational, but the pattern across sites is consistent.

The Android login drop is almost certainly caused by a new vendor rule, not by release 6.14. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC, Corvane's rule-pack update added a rule (AUTO-LIB-17) that blocks password-login requests whose user-agent is 'nettle-http', the library the Android app uses. The first blocks were at 10:41, and the failures began that same minute on every app version. The 6.14 rollout was only 5% of users, and the March security patch made no difference. Quick-unlock is unaffected. About 41,000 blocked installs were real customers; 92% had logged in successfully before. iOS and web were never matched by the rule. Credential-stuffing is not the explanation, and the KPI only counts real app traffic. Do not roll back 6.14, raise bot sensitivity, or exclude blocked attempts from the KPI. Doing so would hide the problem and block more customers. Next step: ask Corvane to set AUTO-LIB-17 to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping other protections on. Then confirm in telemetry that Android password success returns to about 96%. Ask Corvane for a testing and notice process for rule changes. Confidence is high.

The Android login drop is not caused by release 6.14, the password screen, the OS patch, or bots. On 3 March at 10:38 UTC the edge vendor (Corvane) activated a new rule, AUTO-LIB-17. The blocked requests come from about 41,300 install IDs, and 92% of those had logged in successfully in the prior 90 days, so they look like real customers. The failures started within a minute of the rule going live, on every app version and OS version. 6.14 is only 5% of attempts and fails at the same rate as older versions. Quick-unlock and iOS are unaffected. Password success fell from 96.0% to 8.2%.

Next step: ask Corvane to set the new rule to log-only on the mobile password path. Keep rate limits, lockout and other rules on. Then check in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Don't roll back 6.14. Don't raise bot sensitivity. Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI. Either would hide or worsen the problem. Confidence is high. The remaining uncertainty is the contact-centre call rise, which also has other causes.

Do not roll back gateway 5.8. The regression is almost certainly caused by the 2 Nov compaction tuning change on storage nodes, not by the gateway. Per-cell data shows every cell with that change jumped to about 300 ms within minutes of the push, including cells still running 5.7 at the time. The one cell that skipped the change (aps-3) took 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. Rolling euw-1 back to 5.7 changed nothing. After the change, storage disks went from 41% to 97% busy and node-side read time rose from 61 to 262 ms. Network and traffic growth don't explain it, since aps-3 saw the same traffic growth. A rollback would waste about 4 hours, leave the security flaw open, and not fix latency. Next step: revert the tuning in one cell, watch GET p99 and compaction backlog, then extend to the rest. Do not pause compaction, because backlog would build up and risk full disks. The backlog is currently about 4%, well under the 15% danger level, so Orrin rate-limiting can wait for the 10 Nov attribution report. Unknown: what actually drove the earlier backlog growth (Orrin or the cold-tier expiry sweep). Confidence is high on the main cause.

Don't discipline drivers or retrain everyone yet. The evidence points away from driver technique, the hills and the new pads. Northfield also serviced two more vans, which are not in the complaint list. Calder Road Garage fitted the same pads in the same period, and no Calder van shows up. Every Eastgate van ran Upper Wend on 9 to 16 days. The same drivers logged 141 Upper Wend days in non-Northfield vans with no brake reports. Reports were zero in July and August, after the reporting app launched, so easier reporting doesn't explain it. I'm fairly confident, but I haven't seen the Northfield job cards or fluid tests, so the exact fault (probably the brake fluid) is inferred. Next: pull the Northfield-serviced vans from service, boiling-point test the fluid and renew it from sealed stock, and check the two Northfield vans with no complaints. Ask Northfield for their fluid records. Protect the people who reported faults. Leave the pad supplier alone until squeal is checked against fresh pads of the old brand.

The complaints most likely come from contaminated brake fluid, not driver technique or the new routes. Northfield Motor Services used a bulk drum that had been opened in March and had a missing cap. Two vans it serviced and later brought back for a warranty fix tested at 152°C and 149°C boiling point, against 255°C for sealed stock. Water-laden fluid can vaporise on long descents, which gives a soft pedal. All 11 vans with complaints were serviced at Northfield from that drum. The two Northfield vans that got fluid from a new drum had no complaints. The same drivers had no brake reports in other vans on the same hills. Calder Road used the same pads and has no complaint cluster. That counts against the pad, route and reporting-app explanations. Warnings would punish people who reported a real safety fault, and retraining would miss it.

Next steps: pull every Northfield-serviced van out of service now. Test the fluid, renew it from sealed stock, and then return the vans. Cancel the warnings. Tell drivers that reporting is safe. Raise with Northfield why the 25 Sep recheck recommendation got no reply. I'm fairly confident, around 90%. The pad squeal link is unproven, so hold off on changing suppliers for now.

The Android login drop is almost certainly not caused by release 6.14. At 10:38 UTC on 3 March, Corvane auto-updated its edge rules. A new rule, AUTO-LIB-17, blocks any password-login request that uses the nettle-http library with no edge session cookie. That describes every Android app version, because the app uses nettle-http for all API calls. The rule returns a 403. It has blocked about 9,700 requests a day, from roughly 41,300 app installs, 92% of which had logged in successfully before. The failures began within a minute of the rule going live, on every app version and every OS version, whether or not the March security patch was installed. iOS, web and quick-unlock never match the rule. So the rollback of 6.14, the OS patch, the screen redesign, the auth token change and credential stuffing don't explain the drop. I'm quite confident (about 90%). Next: ask Corvane to switch AUTO-LIB-17 to log-only on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockouts and other rules on. Then confirm in telemetry that password success recovers. Don't roll back 6.14. Don't raise bot sensitivity. Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, because those are real customers.

Don't roll back the gateway. The regression comes from the 2 Nov storage compaction tuning change, not from gateway 5.8. That push raised compaction threads from 2 to 6 and compaction's share of disk bytes from 38% to 71%. Disk utilisation went from 41% to 97% within five minutes in each cell. Node-side read time rose from 61 ms to 262 ms. Latency rose in each cell within minutes of its push, even in cells that still had 5.7 or only a few gateways on 5.8. The one cell that skipped the push (aps-3) already had 5.8 and stayed at about 94 ms. A test rollback to 5.7 in euw-1 changed nothing. Rolling back would also reopen the security hole and would not help latency. Network and traffic growth don't fit the timing.

Next: revert the compaction tuning in one cell first, watch p99 and compaction backlog, then extend it to the other cells. Don't pause compaction. Backlog was 11% against a 15% danger point, and a pause risks disk-full. Hold the Orrin rate limit until the 10 Nov attribution report shows where backlog growth comes from. The lifecycle sweep is a competing source. I'm fairly confident in the cause. The Orrin link is the least certain part.

The rise from 0.31% to 0.41% looks like ordinary week-to-week variation, not a fault in v4.18. Over the prior 26 weeks the rate averaged 0.354% with a normal-band upper edge of 0.482%. Weeks hit 0.51%, 0.47% and 0.45% with no fault found, and 0.41% is inside the band. The dashboard count matches raw logs, so it is not a counting artefact. The burn-rate page did not fire (0.82x against a 2x threshold). Booking completion was flat and there were no complaints. The rollout comparison that points at v4.18 is misleading. New pods start with cold caches and time out against the replica in every rollout. That includes an unchanged config-only redeploy and the four earlier releases, at 0.47–0.58% against 0.29–0.33% on old pods. It adds only 10–20 errors. So I would not roll back, and I would not mute the alerts. Muting would remove the protection that would catch a real problem. Record the week as within the normal band and apply the standard check to next week. If next week is above the band or the page fires, open an incident. The replica host change and partner-sync month-end traffic are not ruled out, but nothing here needs action. Confidence is fairly high but not complete.

The Kestria buffering is almost certainly caused by the smart-TV app 5.2 release, not the new CDN. The release lowered the player's startup buffer from 10 s to 4 s and let it switch up in quality after 2 s buffered. It went live in Kestria first, on 9 Oct, the same day as the CDN cutover. Rebuffering on 5.2 TVs is about 5.9% on every ISP. Every other client on the same CDN and ISPs sits at 0.6–0.7%. Employee test TVs in another market, served by the old CDN, showed 5.7% on 5.2 versus 0.6% on 5.1 before launch. The fix for that test was deferred. Handball viewing and ISP congestion don't fit the pattern. Recommendation: don't send the breach notice, withhold fees or move traffic back. That would punish the wrong party and leave the problem in place. Instead, revert Kestria to the old streaming settings (abr_v2 is a server-side remote-config profile, roughly an hour to take effect). Hold the 20 Nov wider rollout, and keep the rebuffering alert on. Then add app version and device breakdowns to monitoring. Hold the free-month offer until you've confirmed how much of the cancellation rise comes from buffering, since the 1 Oct price rise is also a likely factor. I'm confident in the main finding. The cancellation link is unproven.

Keep LK-209 parked until that is done. Tell drivers that reporting is safe. Consider checking the Calder Road vans and pad noise separately.

Jobs before 4 Oct were correct, including those after the firmware change and those set up by agency operators. Two jobs on Line 1 day shift, run by permanent staff, were also wrong. Check other products with October edits, especially the two with later valid-from dates. Ask the vendor to explain the behaviour. I'm fairly sure of the Veltranol cause. Other products are unchecked.
