Analyzer B most likely had a single chance QC outlier. The repeat from the same vial passed. Sodium, chloride and the other two potassium levels were fine. Level 2 means are unchanged since the lot change (5.81 before, 5.80 after). Only one flag appeared in a month, which fits the expected false-rejection rate. B and A agree on 43 patient samples (mean difference +0.02). B's patient median is steady. All 182 scheduled QC runs were completed on time, so the claim that short staffing led to skipped QC is not supported. A short sample or bubble can't be excluded, so don't record it as the confirmed cause.

Ward 6's high potassiums are split evenly between Analyzers A and B. They coincide with the tube outage, which caused long transport delays, and with four renal overflow patients. Delay is the likelier explanation, though that link is only an association so far. No repeat samples were requested.

What to sign off: return B to service and close the 186 results with no amendments. Optionally add extra Level 2 QC for a week. Don't recall results, quarantine the lot or widen the limits. Ask Ward 6 to send repeat samples and fix the tube station. I'm moderately confident in this.

Analyzer B most likely had one isolated potassium QC outlier: a chance flag or a one-off sampling glitch. The evidence points that way for five reasons. The other two QC levels passed. The repeat from the same vial passed. QC means are unchanged since the lot change. All 43 patient samples re-run on Analyzer A agreed within limits. B's patient median is normal. QC ran on schedule, so skipped QC is not supported. The Ward 6 highs are split 7 on A and 7 on B. Most of them had samples more than 3 hours in transit during the tube outage, and four renal overflow patients arrived at the same time. So the analyzers are probably not giving false highs. I'm less sure of the tube-delay explanation, because the renal patients could also account for it.

Recommended sign-off:
- Return B to potassium service and close the review of the 186 results with no amendments.
- Do not recall everything, because that means recollecting about 2,900 patients.
- Do not quarantine the lot.
- Do not widen the limits.
- Don't record a sampling glitch as the confirmed cause. It is only plausible.
- Optionally add extra Level 2 QC per shift for a week.
- Ask Ward 6 to repeat samples on the high results, and fix the tube station.

Confidence is moderate to high. I did not collect any further evidence.

The VA-220 failures trace to Pellacott's 2026-built valves, not to the new installers or firmware 4.2. The quality-lab data matched to serial numbers shows the same claim rate (about 41–42 per 1,000) for legacy and new installers and for firmware 4.1 and 4.2. Durrant-Hale valves stay at 5–7 per 1,000 in every group. Never-installed Pellacott 2026 valves leak at the seat 11% of the time, against 1% for 2025 builds and 0% for Durrant-Hale. The calibration contractor found Pellacott's leak-test rig out of service since January 2026, with no VA-220 test program on any other rig. Certificate values repeat four fixed sequences, which also appear in November 2025 certificates. So the certificates very likely do not reflect real tests. That also explains the score rise, since the score rewarded complete certificates. Do not release the six held lots on fresh certificates, and do not penalise the installers. Quarantine 2026-built Pellacott stock, suspend dock-to-stock, and run your own helium leak testing before release. Plan for line impact by sourcing more from Durrant-Hale. Check whether other suppliers' records are genuine, and tie scoring to rig logs. The seal change is a plausible mechanism but isn't separable from the line move. Confidence is high.

The cancellation rise is not mainly a pricing problem. It is concentrated in accounts connected to Quillbook. Their monthly churn went from about 2% to about 6%, and it is the same for price-locked Founders accounts and repriced accounts. Since then the connector has silently dropped or duplicated 58,300 invoices across 1,212 accounts. 34% of those accounts have cancelled, against 8% of accounts with no recorded failure. The health panel counts only ERROR, so these WARN events were never seen. Support is also slow, but that looks like a side effect.

Recommendation: don't roll back the price, which would cost about $220k a month and wouldn't fix this. Don't switch off the duplicate-invoice hold, because it has kept 3,870 duplicates out of customers' books. Make the Quillbook v3 migration (3–4 weeks) the top engineering priority. Contact every Quillbook account, including those that cancelled, to correct their invoices. Make the health panel count WARN events. Review the Tallymarsh log before committing a rebuild; its churn change is within normal variation. Confidence is fairly high, though this is observational data.

The promotion gap is mostly a tenure effect, not proof of proximity bias. Remote work was opened to all roles only in July 2024, so 230 of 340 remote staff (68%) have under 18 months in level and are ineligible under policy, against 26% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2% remote, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows in every job family, so job mix doesn't explain it. Caveat: only 110 remote staff are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. The interview and survey hints about uneven stretch work and less clarity on promotion criteria remain unverified. Recommendation: don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would exclude about 180 people hired on home-based contracts, and the evidence doesn't support it. Hold it, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Separately, check how stretch assignments are distributed, and consider briefing staff on promotion criteria. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding.

The blocked requests come from about 41,300 install IDs, 92% of which logged in successfully in the previous 90 days, so they look like real customers rather than bots. What to do: don't roll back 6.14, and don't raise bot sensitivity. Raising it would block more real customers. Don't exclude blocked attempts from the KPI, because that would hide a real customer-facing failure. Instead, ask Corvane to put the rules added in 2026.03.1 into log-only mode on the mobile password path, keeping rate limits, lockout and other rules active. Then confirm in telemetry that password success returns to about 96%. Remaining uncertainty: the contact-centre call rise is only loosely tied to the login failures.
